name: Again Trees... (Easy Version)
description: This is the easy version of the problem. The difference between the versions is that in this version, $$$k \leq 4$$$. You can hack only if you solved all versions of this problem. Given a tree consisting of $$$n$$$ vertices. Each vertex has a non-negative integer $$$a_v$$$ written on it. You are also given $$$k$$$ distinct non-negative integers $$$b_1, \ldots, b_k$$$. We will call a set of edges beautiful if, after removing these edges from the tree, the tree splits into connected components, where in each component the bitwise XOR of all the numbers $$$a_v$$$ in that component belongs to the set $$$b$$$. You need to count the number of beautiful sets of edges in the tree modulo $$$10^9 + 7$$$.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 500$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each dataset contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$2 \leq n \leq 10^5$$$, $$$1 \leq k \leq 4$$$) — the number of vertices in the tree and the size of the set $$$b$$$. The next $$$n - 1$$$ lines describe the edges of the tree. The $$$i$$$-th line contains two integers $$$v_i$$$ and $$$u_i$$$ ($$$1 \leq v_i, u_i \leq n$$$) — the numbers of the vertices connected by the $$$i$$$-th edge. The next line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$0 \leq a_i \lt 2^{30}$$$) — the values written on the vertices. The following line contains $$$k$$$ distinct integers $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_k$$$ ($$$0 \leq b_i \lt 2^{30}$$$) — the elements of the set $$$b$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ across all datasets does not exceed $$$10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test dataset, output a single integer — the answer to the problem.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2194F1 — Again Trees... (Easy Version) [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
